name: James Buchanan
role: President of the United States (1857–1861); earlier senator, secretary of state and diplomat
summary: Buchanan defended a strictly limited federal government and the constitutional protection of slavery while opposing a legal right of secession. He supported territorial expansion and selective economic regulation, alongside fiscal economy and state authority over education.

sources.title: State of the Union Addresses, 1857–1860
sources.author: James Buchanan, Project Gutenberg
sources.usedFor: Full collection downloaded and searched by theme: bank regulation, tariffs, land settlement, Indigenous policy and military requests.

sources.author: James Buchanan, Miller Center
sources.usedFor: Secession, coercion, resistance, slavery and constitutional guarantees; also present in downloaded collection.

sources.title: Veto Message, June 22, 1860: Homestead bill
sources.author: James Buchanan, American Presidency Project
sources.usedFor: Full veto downloaded: land grants, dependency, property, native/naturalized citizenship and immigration incentives.

sources.title: Veto Message, February 24, 1859: agricultural colleges
sources.author: James Buchanan, American Presidency Project
sources.usedFor: Full veto downloaded: federal versus state authority over educational funding.

sources.title: Protest Message, March 28, 1860
sources.author: James Buchanan, American Presidency Project
sources.usedFor: Full protest downloaded: coordinate executive and legislative powers, impeachment and congressional investigation.

sources.title: Inaugural Address, March 4, 1857
sources.author: James Buchanan, American Presidency Project
sources.usedFor: Constitutional limits, territorial voting, immigration and land settlement; personal one-term pledge distinguished from term-limit law.

sources.title: Ostend Manifesto, October 18, 1854

notes: No inferred answers. Full annual-message collection, principal domestic vetoes, constitutional protest and 1866 postwar defense were downloaded and searched by theme, with the entire statement list and remaining unknowns checked. Slavery is documented through racial citizenship, unequal legal rights and slave-property protection; it is not automatically equated with land-bound serfdom. His claim that abolitionist agitation caused the rupture is retained as a qualified, low-confidence answer, not adopted as the historical explanation. His later book calls slavery an evil but condemns forcible outside emancipation and does not establish equal political rights. Preserving federal forts is distinguished from coercive war against a state. Neither a personal one-term pledge nor a veto of federal college grants establishes general legal term limits or opposition to tuition-free state colleges. No economic views borrowed from James M. Buchanan. Personal relationships do not establish positions on sexual law. Broad faith, Providence references and constitutional praise do not establish specific church, women’s, ecological or modern technology policies. Native/naturalized equality is not generalized into racial equality. Formal signatures alone are not used; cited proposals and vetoes state his own reasons. General native/naturalized equality does not establish eligibility for every public office, and opposing a homestead immigration incentive does not establish a preferred overall immigration level; both specific statements remain unknown.
